proposals.relationship: As Ian Davey reads the 1988 schooling study, Curtis combines Foucault’s analysis of power and subjectivity with a Marxist account of state formation.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Davey’s 1989 review, printed 161, identifies the combination as an analytical strength, while his criticism of patriarchal relations on 165 remains. Curtis’s complete 1988 book and the particular Foucault originals remain unread; this is a specified theoretical resource, not an exclusive lineage or unqualified agreement.
primary_locators: Davey 1989, printed 161, right column, second paragraph beginning As I have observed elsewhere; printed 165, concluding review paragraph on patriarchal relations.

proposals.relationship: Palmer questions treating Curtis’s school-inspection study as a representative model of Canadian state formation, while crediting its revision of responsible government.
proposals.evidence_note: Fresh primary review, 1993, printed 365–367: Palmer finds the inspection focus too narrow and its model overstated, but acknowledges useful evidence and the responsible-government argument. His separate criticism of Greer and Radforth’s edited collection retains its own subject; the entire joint review is not assigned to Curtis. Curtis’s 1992 book remains unread.
primary_locators: Palmer 1993, printed 365, left column Curtis telescopes paragraph; 366, left column As argument paragraph and right column The single most important contribution; review ends on 367.

proposals.relationship: As Christie and Fecteau report, Curtis questions McKay’s singular liberal project and recommends closer attention to governmentality.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Christie’s 2009 essay, paragraph beginning Since liberalism, attributes the governmentality point to Curtis without identifying his text. Fecteau’s 2009 discussion quotes Curtis’s objections to deterministic identity/action and a unitary project, citing 179 and 184. Curtis’s chapter and McKay’s full reply remain unread; these witnesses are consolidated rather than counted as separate exchanges.
primary_locators: Christie 2009, sixth essay paragraph by count, beginning Since liberalism was a response; Fecteau 2009, numbered discussion items 1 and 2, Curtis 2009 citations to 179 and 184.

proposals.relationship: Curtis credits Elias’s work with shaping his interpretation of state paper collections.
proposals.evidence_note: Undated first-person Carleton research statement, About, paragraph beginning Historians criticized. Other credited resources remain distinct; no particular Elias title, edition or date of transmission is supplied.
primary_locators: Carleton Institute of Political Economy profile, About, second paragraph, Historians criticized my early historical sociology.

proposals.relationship: Curtis names Marx’s sociology among the resources directing his attention to changing social forms and practices.
proposals.evidence_note: Undated first-person Carleton statement, About, paragraph beginning Together with. Simmel, Bourdieu and the previously named resources share credit; this does not make Curtis’s approach wholly Marx’s.
primary_locators: Carleton Institute of Political Economy profile, About, third paragraph, Together with the sociology of Marx, Simmel and Bourdieu.

proposals.relationship: Curtis identifies Bourdieu’s sociology and category slippage as resources for studying social forms and classification.
proposals.evidence_note: Undated first-person Carleton statement, About, paragraphs beginning Together with and I have always. This credits specific analytical interests; the original Bourdieu works remain unread and unnamed.
primary_locators: Carleton Institute of Political Economy profile, About, third and fourth paragraphs, Together with and I have always been fascinated.

proposals.relationship: Curtis objects that political authorities cannot simply discover population, because population depends on the exercise of sovereign authority.
proposals.evidence_note: The substantive authorial abstract of Curtis’s 2002 article, reproduced on ResearchGate, reconstructs Foucault’s usage and states this conceptual objection. Reading is limited to the English/French abstract; the complete article and Foucault originals remain unread. This specific criticism coexists with the separately evidenced Foucault resource and does not establish wholesale rejection.
primary_locators: Curtis 2002, authorial English abstract, final two sentences; corroborating French abstract on same ResearchGate record. DOI 10.2307/3341588; original article505–533, abstract at505.
